sentences.t: Ярославнынъ гласъ слышитъ: зегзицею незнаемь, рано кычеть: полечю, рече, зегзицею по Дунаеви;
sentences.tr: Jaroslavnynŭ glasŭ slyšitŭ: zegziceju neznaemĭ, rano kyčetĭ: polečju, reče, zegziceju po Dunaevi;
sentences.l: One hears Yaroslavna's voice: as a cuckoo unrecognized, early she calls: I will fly, she says, as a cuckoo along the Danube;
sentences.i: Yaroslavna's voice can be heard: unrecognized, like a cuckoo, she cries out at early dawn: 'I will fly,' she says, 'like a cuckoo along the Danube;'
sentences.n: This opens a new source paragraph — the poem's shift from the princes' roll-call (part 6) and the elegy for Vseslav's line (part 7) to Yaroslavna's lament for Igor, its most celebrated passage. «Ярославнынъ» is a possessive adjective, 'Yaroslavna's' (she is Igor's wife, daughter of Yaroslav Osmomysl of Galich met in part 6); «гласъ ... слышитъ», 'one hears [her] voice,' uses слышитъ without the reflexive particle that would mark a true passive in later Russian — an impersonal construction, subject unstated. «зегзицею» is instrumental of зегзица 'cuckoo' (a comparison-instrumental, the same construction used of Boyan's animal transformations in the proem: 'сѣрымъ вълкомъ,' 'шизымъ орломъ'); «незнаемь» is itself uncertain in gender/case (a worn short-form adjective, 'unknown, unrecognized') and its exact attachment is debated, but the sense — Yaroslavna, as if transformed into a bird, calling out unrecognized — is clear enough. The wish to fly as a cuckoo along the Danube to reach and tend Igor's wounds is the poem's one moment of benign shape-shifting, set against Vseslav's sinister wolf-transformations in part 7; the cuckoo (зегзица/зозуля) is a bird long tied in East Slavic folk lament to a woman crying for an absent or dead husband. «рече» (aorist, 'she said') is a parenthetical, framing the direct speech that follows.

sentences.t: омочю бебрянъ рукавъ въ Каялѣ рѣцѣ, утру Князю кровавыя его раны на жестоцѣмъ его тѣлѣ.
sentences.tr: omočju bebrjanŭ rukavŭ vŭ Kajalě rěcě, utru Knjazju krovavyja jego rany na žestocěmŭ jego tělě.
sentences.l: I will wet [my] beaver sleeve in the Kayala river, I will wipe for the Prince his bloody wounds on his harsh body.
sentences.i: I will dip my beaver-fur sleeve in the river Kayala, and wipe clean the Prince's bloody wounds on his battered body.
sentences.n: «бебрянъ рукавъ», a sleeve of/trimmed with beaver fur — a costly, aristocratic detail that heightens the pathos of her fantasy: she would use her own fine sleeve to tend her husband's wounds. Каяла, the river by which Igor's army was routed in 1185, recurs through the poem; its real identity has never been settled despite many proposed identifications with streams of the Donets basin, and none is asserted here. «омочю»/«утру» are 1st-singular non-past forms (perfective 'I will wet'/'I will wipe') continuing the vow begun in unit 1 — a run of first-person future forms that make this opening read as a spoken vow or incantation rather than plain narration. «жестоцѣмъ», 'harsh, hard' (жестокъ, source of modern жестокий 'cruel'), most likely describes Igor's body as battle-hardened or battered by wounds rather than morally 'cruel.'

sentences.t: Ярославна рано плачетъ въ Путивлѣ на забралѣ, аркучи: о вѣтрѣ! вѣтрило! чему Господине насильно вѣеши?
sentences.tr: Jaroslavna rano plačetŭ vŭ Putivlě na zabralě, arkuči: o větrě! větrilo! čemu Gospodine nasilĭno věeši?
sentences.l: Yaroslavna weeps early in Putivl on the rampart, saying: O wind! wind-driver! why, Lord, do you blow so forcefully?
sentences.i: Yaroslavna weeps at early dawn in Putivl, upon the rampart, crying out: 'O Wind! O Wind-driver! Why, my Lord, do you blow with such force?'
sentences.n: The first of the lament's three parallel addresses — to the Wind, the Dnepr (unit 7), and the Sun (unit 9) — each opened by the same refrain, «Ярославна рано плачеть(ъ) [въ/къ] Путивлѣ на забралѣ/заборолѣ, аркучи:» ('Yaroslavna weeps early ... upon the rampart, saying:'), a rhetorical trikolon typical of the older East Slavic плачь (parting/funeral lament) genre — apostrophizing personified natural forces in turn. «аркучи» is a present active participle of an otherwise unattested verb, аркати ('to say, speak'); it occurs nowhere else in Old East Slavic outside this poem. Путивль is Igor's own town, already the setting of his muster in part 1; забрало names the wall-walk/rampart of a fortified town, her vantage point in every telling of this scene. «Господине», vocative, addresses the Wind as if it were a lord — apostrophe to natural forces as willful, personal beings marks this whole passage's folk-incantatory register. «вѣтрило» intensifies «вѣтрѣ» (an emphatic doubling, 'Wind! Wind!') rather than naming something distinct from the wind itself.

sentences.t: Чему мычеши Хиновьскыя стрѣлкы на своею не трудною крилцю на моея лады вои?
sentences.tr: Čemu myčeši Xinovĭskyja strělky na svoeju ne trudnoju krilcju na moeja lady voi?
sentences.l: Why do you toss the Khin arrows, upon your own untoiling wing, upon my dear one's warriors?
sentences.i: Why do you hurl Khin arrows at my beloved's warriors, borne on your own untiring wing?
sentences.n: Хиновьскыя, 'of the Khin' — the same obscure people/name met as «Хинова» in part 6, there flagged as unidentified (perhaps a folk-memory of the Huns, perhaps a name loosely applied later to a distant steppe people); here, in the context of Igor's rout, it most likely stands for Cuman/Polovtsian horse-archers. «на своею не трудною крилцю», 'upon your own untiring wing' — a genuine crux of case and sense (an instrumental-looking phrase attached to a noun that looks dative/locative); the sense generally taken is that the wind, itself unwearied, uses its own effortless strength to carry the enemy's arrows. «лады» (here genitive singular) is usually read from «лада», an old term of endearment for one's own husband — giving 'my dear one's soldiers,' i.e. Igor's men, a reading supported by unit 8's unambiguous «мою ладу», 'my dear one' (accusative, of Igor); but the exact construal of «лады вои» has been contested by editors, with at least one minority proposal connecting the word to a different root entirely, and no single reading is treated here as final.

sentences.t: Мало ли ти бяшетъ горъ подъ облакы вѣяти, лелѣючи корабли на синѣ морѣ?
sentences.tr: Malo li ti bjašetŭ gorŭ podŭ oblaky vějati, lelějuči korabli na sině morě?
sentences.l: Was it too little for you to blow among the mountains beneath the clouds, cradling ships upon the blue sea?
sentences.i: Was it not enough for you to sweep among the mountains under the clouds, rocking ships upon the blue sea?
sentences.n: «Мало ли ти бяшетъ», 'was it too little for you' (a rhetorical formula built on the imperfect of быти), reproaches the Wind for turning from its natural, benign range — over mountains, beneath clouds, across the open sea — to the cruelty of the previous line. «лелѣючи», 'cradling, nursing' (лелѣяти, the same verb that returns as «лелѣялъ», 'you have cradled,' of the Dnepr's boats in unit 8, and «възлелѣй», 'cradle!,' the imperative that follows it there — and that already described the Kurian warriors 'cradled under helmets' in part 1) ties this whole passage together on one image: a nurse's tenderness, either withheld by the Wind or hoped for from the Dnepr.

sentences.t: Чему Господине мое веселіе по ковылію развѣя?
sentences.tr: Čemu Gospodine moe veselie po kovyliju razvěja?
sentences.l: Why, Lord, have you scattered my gladness along the feather-grass?
sentences.i: Why, my Lord, have you blown my joy away across the feather-grass?
sentences.n: «ковылію», feather-grass (ковыль, Stipa) — the characteristic grass of the open steppe, the same terrain over which Igor's host was destroyed; her gladness pictured as scattered like windblown grass-seed over that very steppe gives the image real geographic bite. «развѣя» is an aorist (a single completed action, 'scattered'), set against the surrounding present tenses of the address — marking her joy as already, finally, gone.

sentences.t: Ярославна рано плачеть Путивлю городу на заборолѣ, аркучи: о Днепре словутицю! ты пробилъ еси каменныя горы сквозѣ землю Половецкую.
sentences.tr: Jaroslavna rano plačetĭ Putivlju gorodu na zaborolě, arkuči: o Dnepre slovuticju! ty probilŭ jesi kamennyja gory skvozě zemlju Poloveckuju.
sentences.l: Yaroslavna weeps early, Putivl-town, on the rampart, saying: O Dnepr, renowned one! you have broken through stone mountains, across the Polovtsian land.
sentences.i: Yaroslavna weeps at early dawn in the town of Putivl, upon the rampart, crying out: 'O Dnepr Slovutich! You have cut clean through rocky mountains, straight across the land of the Polovtsians.'
sentences.n: The second address, to the Dnepr, under its traditional honorific epithet «Словутичь» ('the renowned, far-famed one'), an epithet for the river also found elsewhere in Old Rus' writing (e.g. the Primary Chronicle), reflecting its standing as the great river of Rus'. Note the refrain's small print variants against unit 3's wording: «плачеть» (ь) here for unit 3's «плачетъ» (ъ); «Путивлю городу», an unprefixed dative ('at Putivl-town'), for unit 3's prepositional «въ Путивлѣ»; «заборолѣ» for «забралѣ» — small, real spelling inconsistencies of the 1800 print, kept exactly as printed rather than normalized, as elsewhere in this edition. «ты пробилъ еси», 'you have broken through' — a periphrastic perfect (past-tense participle + 2sg «еси», 'you are'), the old way of forming this tense; modern Russian keeps only the participle ('ты пробил') and has long since dropped the person-marking auxiliary, so this construction is easy for a modern reader to miss. «каменныя горы», 'stone/rocky mountains,' may allude to the Dnepr's famous rapids further downstream, where the river cut through granite outcrops on its way toward the Black Sea and the Polovtsian steppe, though the text itself does not say so explicitly.

sentences.t: Ты лелѣялъ еси на себѣ Святославли носады до плъку Кобякова: възлелѣй господине мою ладу къ мнѣ, а быхъ неслала къ нему слезъ на море рано.
sentences.tr: Ty lelějalŭ jesi na sebě Svjatoslavli nosady do plŭku Kobjakova: vŭzlelěj gospodine moju ladu kŭ mně, a byxŭ neslala kŭ nemu slezŭ na more rano.
sentences.l: You have cradled upon yourself Svyatoslav's boats, as far as Kobyak's host: cradle, O Lord, my dear one back to me, so that I would not send to him my tears upon the sea, early.
sentences.i: You bore Svyatoslav's boats upon your own waters, all the way to Kobyak's camp — cradle my beloved back to me now, my Lord, so that I need not send my tears out to him over the sea at dawn.
sentences.n: «носады», a type of shallow-draft Rus' river boat used on campaigns down the Dnepr. «до плъку Кобякова» anchors the line in real history: Svyatoslav Vsevolodovich of Kiev — the same Svyatoslav of the Golden Word in parts 5–6 — led a real campaign down the Dnepr in 1183 that defeated and captured the Polovtsian khan Kobyak, recorded in the Hypatian Chronicle; Yaroslavna wishes the river had carried her own husband as safely as it once carried that expedition. «възлелѣй», an imperative built on the same лелѣяти root as unit 5's «лелѣючи», turns the cradling-image into a direct plea. «а быхъ неслала» is a conditional/purpose construction (быхъ, an old aorist-derived conditional auxiliary — ancestor of modern 'бы' — with the past-tense participle неслала): 'so that I would not [have to] send/carry.' «мою ладу», 'my dear one' (accusative), unambiguously names Igor by the same endearment debated in unit 4's «лады».

sentences.t: Ярославна рано плачетъ къ Путивлѣ на забралѣ, аркучи: свѣтлое и тресвѣтлое слънце! всѣмъ тепло и красно еси:
sentences.tr: Jaroslavna rano plačetŭ kŭ Putivlě na zabralě, arkuči: světloe i tresvětloe slŭnce! vsěmŭ teplo i krasno jesi:
sentences.l: Yaroslavna weeps early, at Putivl, on the rampart, saying: bright and thrice-bright sun! to all are you warm and fair:
sentences.i: Yaroslavna weeps at early dawn, at Putivl, upon the rampart, crying out: 'O bright, thrice-bright sun! To everyone you are warm and beautiful —
sentences.n: The third and final address, to the Sun, framed by the same refrain, with its own small print variant — «плачетъ» as in unit 3, but «къ Путивлѣ» (a preposition normally governing the dative used here before what looks like a locative ending), likely a further variant or slip for unit 3's «въ Путивлѣ»; kept exactly as printed. «тресвѣтлое», 'thrice-bright' (тре- 'three-' + свѣтлое 'bright'), is an intensifying compound found nowhere else in the poem; whether it carries any further resonance is not something the text itself confirms. «тепло и красно еси», 'you are warm and fair,' uses short-form (nominal) neuter adjectives agreeing with the sun's grammatical gender even though the sun is addressed in the 2nd person — a predicate pattern modern Russian no longer forms this way; «красно» here means 'beautiful, fair' (the older sense of красный), not 'red.'

sentences.t: чему господине простре горячюю свою лучю на ладѣ вои?
sentences.tr: čemu gospodine prostre gorjačjuju svoju lučju na ladě voi?
sentences.l: why, Lord, have you spread your hot ray upon [my] dear one's warriors?
sentences.i: why, my Lord, have you cast your scorching ray upon my beloved's warriors?
sentences.n: «простре», 'stretched forth,' appears to be a bare aorist (2nd singular) rather than the periphrastic perfect used of the Dnepr's feats in unit 7 («пробилъ еси») and unit 8 («лелѣялъ еси») — the poet moves between the two past-tense constructions without any change of meaning, a genuine feature of the language's flexibility rather than an error. «на ладѣ вои» repeats unit 4's disputed phrase «на моея лады вои» in the same sense ('upon my dear one's soldiers'), but spelled «ладѣ» rather than «лады» — one more small, real orthographic inconsistency of the 1800 print for the same word and case, kept here exactly as printed rather than silently regularized.

sentences.t: въ полѣ безводнѣ жаждею имь лучи съпряже, тугою имъ тули затче.
sentences.tr: vŭ polě bezvodně žaždeju imĭ luči sŭprjaže, tugoju imŭ tuli zatče.
sentences.l: in the waterless field, with thirst he bound their rays together for them; with anguish he stopped up their quivers for them.
sentences.i: In the waterless field he fused their rays with thirst; with anguish he sealed their quivers shut.
sentences.n: The lament, and this part, close on a concrete, historically grounded image: chronicle accounts of Igor's 1185 campaign describe his army suffering severe thirst in the open steppe in the days before its final defeat by the Kayala. «лучи», 'rays,' is kept as printed, continuing the sun's-ray imagery of unit 10; some editors instead read «луки», 'bows,' which would parallel «тули», 'quivers,' in the next clause as a second piece of military gear ruined by the ordeal rather than a continuation of the solar image — neither reading is asserted here as certain. «тули затче», 'stopped up/plugged the quivers,' is itself debated in sense: it may picture the quivers as physically jammed or unusable, or figure the men's own strength and will to fight as stopped, exhausted by grief and thirst. «съпряже» and «затче» are both aorist third-singular forms (completed past action), closing the passage, like unit 6's «развѣя», on a note of finality.
